title: Chapter 6: Model-View-Controller (MVC) Pattern
description: This lesson covers the Model-View-Controller (MVC) design pattern in Human-Computer Interaction, detailing the functions of the Model, View, and Controller, interaction flow, software maintenance benefits, and quick analogies.
content:
Introduction to Model-View-Controller (MVC)

Model–View–Controller (MVC) is a design pattern in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) and software design.

It divides a system into three parts:

  • Model: the brain (data & logic)
  • View: the face (what you see)
  • Controller: the hands (what you do)

Purpose: To make programs easier to build, understand, and fix.

Think of MVC like a restaurant:

  • Model: kitchen (where the food is prepared = data/logic)
  • View: menu + food served (what the customer sees)
  • Controller: waiter (takes your order and delivers it between kitchen and you)

Core Components of MVC

1. Model (The Brain of the System)

Stores and manages the system’s data and rules.

Function:

  • Knows everything about the system’s content.
  • Updates data when something changes.
  • Does not care about how things look on screen.

Without the Model, the program has no knowledge to show.

2. View (The Face of the System)

The visual representation of the data.

Function:

  • Shows information to the user in a friendly way.
  • Changes automatically when the Model updates.

Without the View, users can’t see or interact with the data.

3. Controller (The Hands of the System)

Acts as a bridge between the user and the system.

Function:

  • Takes input from the user (clicks, taps, voice, typing).
  • Decides what action to perform.
  • Tells the Model or View what to do.

Without the Controller, the user cannot communicate with the system.

How MVC Works Together (Flow)

  1. User does something (click, tap, type) -> handled by Controller.
  2. Controller updates the Model (changes data).
  3. Model notifies the View of changes.
  4. View shows the updated information to the User.

Benefits of MVC

  • Separation of roles: Each part has its own job.
  • Easy to maintain: Designers can work on View, programmers on Model.
  • Reusability: One Model can work with different Views.
  • Flexibility: Changes in one part don’t break the others.

Quick Analogy Recap

  • Restaurant: Kitchen (Model), Waiter (Controller), Served food (View).
  • Human body: Brain (Model), Hands (Controller), Face (View).
  • Music app: Song data (Model), Playlist screen (View), Play button (Controller).

Remember: MVC is like teamwork. Each part has its own responsibility, and together they make the system run smoothly.

title: Chapter 5: Usability and User Experience Evaluation
description: Covers usability and user experience (UX) evaluation criteria, methods including interviews, cognitive walkthroughs, and Nielsen's heuristics, measurement, and safety and ethics in HCI.
content:
Evaluation Criteria

Usability

Usability is about how easy, efficient, and effective a system is to use.

  • Quantitative: Measured through performance tasks (e.g., how many clicks, how much time it takes to complete an action).
  • Qualitative: Based on user opinions, feedback, and surveys (e.g., how simple or tiring the system feels).
  • Usability Survey: Often includes questions involving the ease of use, ease of learning, fatigue, simple preference, and other questions specific to the given interface.

User Experience (UX)

UX is more than usability it’s about the overall feeling, satisfaction, and emotional connection users have while interacting with the system. Covers how enjoyable, intuitive, and stress-free the app feels.

Evaluation Methods

Interview / Observation

The simplest way: talk to users or watch them use the system. Helps identify problems that designers might miss.

Cognitive Walkthrough

Users “think aloud” while using the system. They describe what they are doing and why. This reveals their thought process and points of confusion.

Expert Heuristic Evaluation

Usability experts review the system using established principles called heuristics.

Nielsen’s ten General UI heuristics:

  1. Visibility of system status
  2. Match between system and the real world
  3. User control and freedom
  4. Consistency and standards
  5. Error prevention
  6. Recognition rather than recall
  7. Flexibility and efficiency of use
  8. Aesthetic and minimalist design
  9. Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
  10. Help and documentation

Measurement

Collect numerical or survey-based data to measure effectiveness. Can involve time, error rates, or satisfaction scores.

Safety & Ethics

Evaluations must be safe and respectful. Users should give informed consent before participating. Participants should always have the right to stop whenever they feel uncomfortable.

Summary

Evaluating a user interface ensures that:

  • The system is easy to use (usability)
  • The experience is positive and enjoyable (UX)
  • The process is safe, ethical, and user-centered
